subtitulo: Venizelos, the Balkan Wars, and the National Schism that split Greece in two (1897–1918)

coda.heading: Resonances 2024–2026 and coda for the trip
intro: The contemporary resonance of the Schism is polarization. Greece has spent a century demonstrating that a political fracture can outlive the problems that gave rise to it and become an inherited identity, passed down through families, towns, and surnames. During the 2010–2015 crisis, a polarization of comparable intensity reappeared — memorandum versus anti-memorandum — which fragmented the party system, and although a recomposition took place from 2019 onward, institutional distrust as measured by European surveys remains among the highest in the Union. The lesson for Peru is uncomfortable: fractures do not close because circumstances change; they close when some generation explicitly decides to close them, as Greece did with the monarchy in 1974, and even then they leave sediment.

items.text: For the trip, three things. In Corfu, the island of Vido: there are regular boats from the old port, the crossing takes fifteen minutes, and the Serbian mausoleum is signposted. Go, even if only for an hour. And the Serbian Museum in the city, small and free or nearly so. It is probably the most politically dense place on your itinerary, and it appears in no standard guidebook.

Second, watch who visits those places. Corfu receives significant Serbian tourism, and for reasons you now understand: it is not only about the beach, it is national pilgrimage. That a vacation destination should simultaneously be a founding cemetery for another nation is an ethnographic phenomenon of the first order.

Third, in Athens, the War Museum and the iconography of Venizelos, whose statue stands on Vasilissis Sofias Avenue. He is the most divisive figure in modern Greek history: for some, the statesman who doubled the country; for others, the man who split it in two and led it to the catastrophe of 1922. Both things are true, and the next installment explains how.

sections.heading: A Cretan in Athens
paragraphs: The humiliation of 1897 produced, twelve years late, a military intervention: in August 1909, a group of officers organized in the Military League rose up at the Goudi barracks on the outskirts of Athens, demanding reforms and the purging of royal-family influence from the army. The officers did not want to govern, and they sought a civilian politician to carry out the program. They brought in Eleftherios Venizelos, a lawyer from Crete.

His origin matters. Crete was not yet part of Greece: it was an autonomous Ottoman province under international supervision following the nineteenth-century revolts, and Venizelos had been formed in that insular politics of permanent insurrection and negotiation with the powers. He arrived in Athens as an outsider to the capital's clienteles, with no debts owed to the notables or to the court, and with a legitimacy built elsewhere. He was prime minister from 1910 and dominated Greek politics for twenty-five years.

His program was the most ambitious effort at state reform since Kapodistrias: a new constitution in 1911, labor and trade-union legislation, a progressive income tax, agrarian reform in the Peloponnese and Thessaly that began dismantling the great estates, reorganization of the army with a French military mission and of the navy with a British one, and an active diplomacy weaving Balkan alliances. Within a few years, a humiliated country became militarily competent.

sections.heading: 1912–1913: a country that doubles and stops being homogeneous
paragraphs: The Balkan Wars were two. In the first, between October 1912 and May 1913, the league of Serbia, Bulgaria, Greece, and Montenegro expelled the Ottoman Empire from almost all of its European territory. In the second, in the summer of 1913, the victors fell out over the spoils, and Bulgaria was defeated by its former allies.

Greece obtained southern Macedonia with Thessaloniki, Epirus with Ioannina, Crete, and the islands of the northeastern Aegean. Its territory and population practically doubled: from about two million seven hundred thousand inhabitants to nearly four million eight hundred thousand. The capture of Thessaloniki in October 1912, mere hours before Bulgarian troops arrived, was a literal race for the most important city in the north.

And here is the problem the victory created. Until 1912, the Greek kingdom had been fairly homogeneous ethnically and religiously, precisely because the wars of 1821–1830 had eliminated the Muslim population. The annexed territories, by contrast, were a mosaic: Macedonia held Greeks, Bulgarians, Muslims of various languages, Vlachs, Albanians; Thessaloniki had a Sephardic community that for centuries had been the city's most numerous group, with its own press in Judeo-Spanish, its own unions, and its own life. Ioannina and Epirus had Albanian Muslims.

A national state built on the ethnolinguistic definition we examined in installment 13 had just annexed populations that did not fit that definition. The response was what the literature calls NATIONALIZATION OF TERRITORY: changing place names, compulsory schooling in Greek, control of property, colonization with Greek population, and, later, the forced population exchange of 1923. It is the classic sequence that produced the Balkan tragedies of the twentieth century, and its logic was inscribed in the definition of nation adopted a century earlier. Here one sees the cost of the road not taken, Rigas's road.

sections.heading: The National Schism: when foreign policy splits a country
paragraphs: The First World War produced in Greece a fracture that dominated its political life for sixty years, and it is worth understanding well because it has no exact equivalent in Latin America, though its shape does.

Venizelos wanted to enter the war alongside the Entente, calculating that an Allied victory would allow the country to claim Ottoman territories and finally achieve the Megali Idea. King Constantine I, militarily trained in Germany and married to a sister of the Kaiser, preferred neutrality and trusted in a German victory. The dispute was not protocolary: it pitted two conceptions of the national interest against each other, with two social bases — the commercial bourgeoisie and the populations of the new territories with Venizelos; the traditional army, the court apparatus, and part of the old peasantry with the king.

The outcome was the DICHASMOS, the Schism. In 1916 Venizelos formed a parallel government in Thessaloniki, with its own army and its own administration, backed by France and Great Britain, while the king governed from Athens. There were two simultaneous Greek states for more than a year. The Allies blockaded the south of the country, there were armed clashes in Athens in December 1916, and in June 1917 they forced the king out. Venizelos reunified the country and brought it into the war on the Allied side. Purges of royalist officials and officers followed, and when the royalists returned to power in 1920 they purged the Venizelists. And so on for decades.

What is sociologically relevant is that this cleavage WAS NOT A CLASS CLEAVAGE. It cut across classes and divided them by external alignment and institutional loyalty — monarchy or republic, Entente or neutrality — and that division structured everything: who got public employment, who was promoted in the army, who was persecuted. It survived the Second World War, fed the civil war of 1946–49, and only dissolved with the 1974 referendum that abolished the monarchy.

The Peruvian parallel is not exact but it is illuminating: the Aprista/anti-Aprista cleavage, which dominated Peruvian politics from 1930 to the 1980s, was also not, strictly speaking, a class cleavage — APRA had a popular base and so did anti-Aprismo — and it organized access to the state, military careers, and repression in the same way. And in the present, the fracture that orders Peruvian politics — and much of Latin American politics — is also not primarily one of class: it is an identity-based alignment and a stance toward the established order that cuts across strata. The cleavages that last longest tend not to be the economic ones.

sections.heading: Corfu, 1916–1917: where Yugoslavia was founded
paragraphs: Now an episode that belongs directly to your itinerary and that almost no one knows.

In the winter of 1915–1916, the Serbian army, defeated by the Austro-German and Bulgarian offensive, undertook a retreat across the mountains of Albania in the depths of winter, together with tens of thousands of civilians. The survivors reached the Adriatic and were evacuated by Allied ships to Corfu: around one hundred fifty thousand soldiers, exhausted, starving, and ill.

Those who could not be saved died on the island and on the neighboring islets. Since there was no space or means to bury them, thousands of bodies were thrown into the sea off the island of Vido, facing the port of Corfu. Serbian tradition calls that place the BLUE TOMB, and Milutin Bojić's poem of that title is one of the foundational texts of Serbian national memory. There is a mausoleum on Vido and a Serbian museum in the city of Corfu, and delegations and visitors arrive from Serbia every year.

And there is more. On July 20, 1917, in Corfu, the Serbian government-in-exile and the Yugoslav Committee signed the DECLARATION OF CORFU, the document that established the principle of a common state of Serbs, Croats, and Slovenes under the Karadjordjević dynasty. Yugoslavia — a state that would exist for seventy-four years, whose dissolution in the 1990s produced the worst European wars since 1945 — was agreed upon on the island you are about to visit.

Consider the density of that. An island that was never Ottoman, that was Venetian for four centuries, British for half a century, incorporated into Greece as a diplomatic gift in 1864, is the place where the Yugoslav state was founded and where an entire army lies buried in the sea. The periphery is not where nothing happens: it is where things happen without anyone recording them in the central narrative.

sections.heading: The simultaneous world: 1919 in Lima and in Smyrna
paragraphs: These years are those of the First World War, the Russian Revolution of 1917, the Mexican Revolution, the 1918 flu, and the dissolution of four empires — Ottoman, Austro-Hungarian, Russian, and German. The Versailles order redrew the map by applying the principle of nationalities, that is, the same ethnic logic Greece had adopted in 1830, with the same results wherever populations were mixed.

In Peru, 1919 opens the Oncenio of Augusto B. Leguía: eleven years of personalist government, public works financed with massive North American borrowing, Patria Nueva rhetoric, constitutional recognition of indigenous communities in 1920 alongside the reinstatement of the road-labor conscription that forced them to work without pay on highways. And in 1928, Mariátegui's Seven Interpretive Essays is published and APRA is founded in Mexico: the two projects that would structure Peruvian politics for the century. Greece and Peru simultaneously live their moment of authoritarian modernizing reform and their moment of founding enduring political traditions.

And there is one final symmetry worth planting here. In May 1919, with Allied authorization, Greek troops landed at Smyrna. That landing, decided at the Paris conferences, begins the sequence that in three years will end in the greatest catastrophe of modern Greek history. It is the subject of the next installment.
